title: Caching: Prompt & Semantic
summary: Agents repeat work constantly — the same system prompt, the same questions, near-duplicate queries — so caching is one of the biggest cost and latency levers. Three layers stack: an exact-match response cache skips the model when the same request repeats; provider prompt caching reuses a stable prefix to cut input-token cost; and a semantic cache embeds the query and reuses the answer for near-duplicates within a similarity threshold. Each needs a TTL and an invalidation strategy so you never serve stale answers.

subtopics.title: Exact-match response cache skips the model entirely
subtopics.explanation: The cheapest cache keys on the exact request (prompt plus params) and stores the model's response; on a repeat, you return it without any model call. It only hits when the request is byte-for-byte identical, so it's ideal for deterministic, high-repeat lookups. This is the first layer to add because it's simple and eliminates whole calls, not just tokens.

subtopics.title: Provider prompt caching reuses a stable prefix
subtopics.explanation: Providers can cache the processed form of a long, unchanging prefix — a big system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples — so repeated calls only pay full price for the changing suffix. You structure messages so the stable content comes first and mark it as cacheable. This cuts input-token cost on every call that shares the prefix, which is most of an agent's traffic.
subtopics.example:
# put the large, unchanging content FIRST so it can be cached
messages = [
    {"role": "system",
     "content": BIG_SYSTEM_PROMPT + TOOL_SCHEMAS,   # stable prefix
     "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},        # mark cacheable
    {"role": "user", "content": user_question},      # changing suffix
]
resp = client.messages.create(messages=messages)
# repeated calls reuse the cached prefix -> cheaper input tokens

subtopics.title: Semantic cache reuses answers for near-duplicates
subtopics.explanation: Two questions can mean the same thing with different words, which an exact-match cache misses. A semantic cache embeds the query into a vector, searches for the nearest stored query, and if similarity clears a threshold, returns that cached answer. It captures paraphrases the exact cache can't, dramatically raising hit rate for open-ended user questions.
subtopics.example:
import numpy as np

store = []   # list of (embedding, answer)

def semantic_get(query, threshold=0.92):
    q = embed(query)                       # vector for the new query
    for vec, answer in store:
        sim = np.dot(q, vec)               # cosine sim (unit vectors)
        if sim >= threshold:               # close enough to reuse
            return answer
    return None

def semantic_put(query, answer):
    store.append((embed(query), answer))

subtopics.title: TTLs and invalidation keep answers fresh
subtopics.explanation: A cached answer can go stale — prices change, docs update, policies shift — so every entry carries a time-to-live and is dropped or refreshed when it expires. You also invalidate explicitly when the underlying data changes (a write, a new document, a version bump). Getting TTL and invalidation right is what separates a cache that saves money from one that quietly serves wrong answers.

subtopics.title: Layer the caches: exact, then prompt, then semantic
subtopics.explanation: The three caches complement rather than replace each other: check the exact-match cache first (free, zero risk of a wrong answer), rely on provider prompt caching for every call that shares a prefix, and fall back to the semantic cache for paraphrased misses. Ordering them cheapest-and-safest first maximizes hit rate while keeping the small correctness risk of semantic matching last. Layering is how production agents get high cache hit rates without ever serving a confidently wrong reused answer.
subtopics.example:
def answer(query, **params):
    hit = exact_cache_get(query, params)      # 1) free, exact
    if hit is not None:
        return hit
    hit = semantic_get(query)                 # 2) paraphrase reuse
    if hit is not None:
        return hit
    # 3) real call still benefits from provider prompt caching
    resp = model.generate(query, **params)
    exact_cache_put(query, params, resp)
    semantic_put(query, resp)
    return resp

foundations.overview: Caching is one of the highest-leverage optimizations for a production agent because so much of its traffic is repetitive: the same large system prompt on every call, the same deterministic lookups, and streams of near-duplicate user questions. Three distinct layers address different kinds of repetition. An exact-match response cache keys on the full request (prompt plus parameters) and returns a stored response verbatim on a byte-identical repeat, eliminating the model call entirely — the cheapest and safest layer. Provider prompt caching operates at the token level: it caches the processed representation of a stable prefix (system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples) so repeated calls that share that prefix pay full price only for the changing suffix, cutting input-token cost across nearly all of an agent's traffic. A semantic cache handles the hardest case — paraphrases — by embedding the query into a vector, finding the nearest stored query, and reusing its answer when similarity clears a threshold, which captures hits an exact cache can never see. The critical discipline across all three is freshness: every entry needs a time-to-live and an explicit invalidation path when the underlying data changes, because a cache that serves stale answers is worse than no cache. In production you layer them cheapest-and-safest first (exact, then prompt caching on the real call, then semantic as a fallback), which maximizes hit rate while keeping the small correctness risk of similarity matching contained.
foundations.formalDefinition: Caching for agents is the reuse of prior computation across three layers: an exact-match cache mapping a hashed request to a stored response; provider prompt caching that reuses the processed form of a stable message prefix to reduce input-token cost; and a semantic cache that reuses a stored answer when an embedding of the new query is within a similarity threshold of a stored query — each governed by a TTL and an invalidation policy.
foundations.whyItMatters: Repeated work is pure waste: it costs full price and full latency to recompute an answer the system already has. Caching removes whole model calls (exact/semantic) and input-token cost (prompt caching), often the largest single cost reduction available, while TTL and invalidation ensure the savings never come at the price of serving stale or wrong answers.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an expert answering questions. An exact-match cache is a sticky note for a question worded identically to one they answered before — instant, verbatim. Prompt caching is the expert already having the reference binder open, so they don't re-read it for each new question. A semantic cache is recognizing 'this is basically the same question I just answered, phrased differently' and reusing that answer. The TTL is a reminder that prices and facts change, so old notes eventually get thrown away and re-derived.
foundations.realWorldUsage: FAQ and support agents caching common answers, RAG systems caching a large stable system prompt and tool schemas via provider prompt caching, high-traffic assistants adding a semantic cache to absorb paraphrased questions, and pipelines invalidating cached answers on document updates or data writes.
foundations.performanceImpact: Exact and semantic hits skip the model call entirely, removing both its latency and cost; provider prompt caching leaves the call but cuts input-token cost sharply on shared prefixes. The tradeoffs are memory for the caches, embedding cost per query for the semantic layer, and a small risk of stale or over-eager matches controlled by TTL and the similarity threshold.
commonUseCases: Exact-match caching of deterministic, high-repeat requests
Provider prompt caching of a large stable system prompt and tool schemas
Semantic caching to absorb paraphrased near-duplicate questions
TTL plus event-driven invalidation on underlying data changes

commonMisconceptions.reality: The three layers catch different repetition — exact bytes, shared prefixes, and paraphrases. Exact caching misses paraphrases; prompt caching still makes the call; semantic caching risks wrong matches. They complement rather than replace each other.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A cache without a TTL is fine if answers rarely change.
commonMisconceptions.reality: 'Rarely' is not 'never' — prices, docs, and policies do change. Without a TTL or invalidation on data writes, a cache silently serves stale answers, which is often worse than paying to recompute.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Semantic caching is just exact caching with embeddings.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It returns an answer for a different but similar query, so an overly low threshold serves subtly wrong answers. It carries a correctness risk (and embedding cost) that exact caching does not, which is why it sits last in the layering.

interactiveExamples.title: Exact-match cache with a hashed key
interactiveExamples.explanation: Key the request on a stable hash of the prompt plus parameters so identical requests hit the cache and skip the model. A counter on the fake model proves the second identical call makes no model call.

code.caption: Two identical requests make one model call; changing a parameter changes the key and forces a fresh call.

interactiveExamples.title: Semantic cache with a similarity threshold and TTL
interactiveExamples.explanation: Embed the query, reuse a stored answer when cosine similarity clears the threshold, and expire entries past their TTL. A tiny fake embedder maps paraphrases to near-identical vectors so a reworded question hits the cache.

code.code:
import time
import numpy as np

def embed(text):
    # fake embedder: paraphrases share the same keyword set -> close vectors
    vocab = ["reset", "password", "refund", "order"]
    v = np.array([1.0 if w in text.lower() else 0.0 for w in vocab])
    n = np.linalg.norm(v)
    return v / n if n else v

store = []   # (embedding, answer, expires_at)

def semantic_get(query, threshold=0.9, now=None):
    now = now or time.time()
    q = embed(query)
    for vec, answer, exp in store:
        if exp > now and float(np.dot(q, vec)) >= threshold:
            return answer                 # near-duplicate within TTL
    return None

def semantic_put(query, answer, ttl_s=300):
    store.append((embed(query), answer, time.time() + ttl_s))

semantic_put("How do I reset my password?", "Use the reset link.")
print(semantic_get("How can I reset the password?"))   # paraphrase -> hit
print(semantic_get("Where is my refund order?"))        # different -> miss
code.caption: The reworded password question clears the threshold and reuses the cached answer; an unrelated query misses.

codeLab.title: Build a TTL cache with explicit invalidation
codeLab.instructions: Implement a TTLCache class with methods get(key), put(key, value, ttl_s), and invalidate(prefix). get returns the stored value only if it exists and has not expired (evicting it if expired, returning None). put stores the value with an expiry of now + ttl_s. invalidate removes every entry whose key starts with the given prefix (used when underlying data changes). Use the injectable self._now() for the current time so the harness can control the clock. Complete the class so the harness passes.
codeLab.testHarness:
c = TTLCache()
clock = {"t": 1000.0}
c._now = lambda: clock["t"]

c.put("user:1:name", "Ada", ttl_s=60)
assert c.get("user:1:name") == "Ada"

# advance past the TTL -> expired
clock["t"] = 1000.0 + 61
assert c.get("user:1:name") is None

# invalidation by prefix
c.put("user:1:name", "Ada", ttl_s=60)
c.put("user:1:email", "a@x.io", ttl_s=60)
c.put("user:2:name", "Lin", ttl_s=60)
c.invalidate("user:1:")
assert c.get("user:1:name") is None
assert c.get("user:1:email") is None
assert c.get("user:2:name") == "Lin"
print("all tests passed")
hints: Store each value as a (value, expires_at) tuple so get can compare expiry against self._now().
In get, if the entry is expired, pop it from the store before returning None so stale entries don't linger.
For invalidate, build the list of matching keys first (don't mutate the dict while iterating it), then pop each.

checkpoints.prompt: What does provider prompt caching reduce?
options: Input-token cost for a shared stable prefix across repeated calls
checkpoints.explanation: Prompt caching reuses the processed form of a stable prefix (system prompt, tool schemas), so repeated calls pay full price only for the changing suffix. The model call still happens — it lowers input-token cost, not call count.

theory.question: What are the three caching layers for an agent, and what does each optimize?
theory.directAnswer: An exact-match response cache keys on the full request and returns a stored answer on a byte-identical repeat, removing the model call entirely. Provider prompt caching reuses the processed form of a stable prefix (system prompt, tool schemas) so shared-prefix calls pay full input-token price only for the changing suffix. A semantic cache embeds the query and reuses a stored answer when similarity clears a threshold, catching paraphrases the exact cache misses.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three complementary reuse layers operating on exact requests, shared token prefixes, and semantically similar queries respectively.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Agent traffic is highly repetitive at different granularities — identical requests, shared prompts, and reworded questions — and each layer captures one kind of repetition the others cannot.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Check the exact cache first (free, zero risk), rely on provider prompt caching on any real call that shares a prefix, and fall back to a semantic cache (embed, nearest-neighbor, threshold) for paraphrased misses, with a TTL and invalidation on every stored answer.

theory.whyImportant: Layering maximizes hit rate — and thus cost and latency savings — while keeping the small correctness risk of similarity matching contained to the last layer.
theory.realWorldExample: A support agent serves identical FAQs from the exact cache, reuses a huge stable system prompt via prompt caching on every call, and absorbs reworded questions with a semantic cache, cutting spend sharply.

followUps.question: Why order them exact, then prompt, then semantic?
followUps.answer: Exact is free and cannot be wrong; prompt caching applies to any real call; semantic is last because it carries a correctness risk and an embedding cost per query.

followUps.question: Does prompt caching skip the model call?
followUps.answer: No — the call still happens; it only reuses the processed prefix to lower input-token cost, unlike exact/semantic hits which skip the call entirely.

theory.question: How do you keep a cache from serving stale answers?
theory.directAnswer: Give every entry a time-to-live so it expires and is recomputed after a bounded age, and add explicit invalidation that drops affected entries the moment the underlying data changes — a write, a new document, a version bump. The TTL bounds worst-case staleness passively; invalidation removes it actively on known changes.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A freshness policy combining passive expiry (TTL) with active, event-driven invalidation of affected keys.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Cached answers reflect the state at cache time; prices, documents, and policies change, so without expiry or invalidation the cache silently returns outdated answers.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Store each entry with an expires_at timestamp and evict on read when expired; on a data-changing event, invalidate by key or prefix so all dependent cached answers are removed and recomputed on next request.

theory.whyImportant: A stale answer served confidently can be worse than no cache at all, so freshness control is what makes caching safe to deploy, not just cheap.
theory.realWorldExample: A pricing agent cached quotes with a short TTL and also invalidated the product's cache key on any price write, so a price change was reflected immediately rather than after the TTL elapsed.

followUps.question: How do you pick a TTL?
followUps.answer: Match it to how fast the underlying data changes and your staleness tolerance — short for volatile data (prices), long for stable content (docs), and lean on invalidation for changes you can detect.

followUps.question: What's the risk of an aggressive semantic threshold with caching?
followUps.answer: Too low a threshold reuses answers for questions that only look similar, serving wrong answers; keep the threshold conservative and combine with TTL.

scenario.question: Your support agent's costs are high and users often ask the same thing in different words. You add a semantic cache and costs drop, but users start reporting occasional wrong answers. How do you diagnose and fix it while keeping the savings?
scenario.directAnswer: The wrong answers come from the semantic cache matching queries that are similar but not equivalent, so raise the similarity threshold, log every semantic hit with its similarity score and the served answer, and sample them for correctness. Keep the exact-match and prompt-caching layers (which are safe), tighten the threshold until wrong matches disappear, and add a TTL plus invalidation so updated answers aren't reused past their validity.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cache-correctness problem caused by an over-eager semantic similarity threshold combined with missing staleness controls.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Embedding similarity is a proxy for meaning; a threshold set too low treats distinct questions as the same, and without TTL/invalidation even correct reuses can go stale.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Instrument semantic hits with their scores, review the low-scoring hits that produced wrong answers, raise the threshold above that band, and layer exact caching first so only genuine paraphrases reach the semantic layer, all under a TTL with event-driven invalidation.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows how to capture caching's cost savings without sacrificing correctness — the central tension of semantic caching in production.
scenario.realWorldExample: Logs showed wrong answers clustered at similarity 0.85-0.90; raising the threshold to 0.94 and adding a TTL eliminated the bad reuses while keeping most of the cost reduction from true paraphrase hits.

followUps.question: Why not remove the semantic cache entirely?
followUps.answer: It captures a large share of paraphrased traffic the exact cache misses; tuning the threshold keeps those savings while removing the wrong matches.

followUps.question: How would you catch a future regression?
followUps.answer: Alert on the semantic-hit distribution and periodically sample hits against fresh model answers, so a drift in embeddings or content shows up before users report it.

coding.question: Write a layered answer(query) that checks an exact cache first, then a semantic cache (embedding + cosine threshold), and only calls the model on a miss — storing the result in both caches.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want the cheapest, safest layer first, so I check the exact cache (a dict keyed by the raw query) before doing any embedding work. On an exact miss I embed the query and scan the semantic store for a match above the threshold. Only if both miss do I call the model, then write the answer to both caches so future exact and paraphrased repeats hit. I keep cosine similarity simple by assuming unit vectors from the embedder.

solution.code:
import numpy as np

exact = {}                 # query -> answer
sem_store = []             # list of (embedding, answer)

def embed(text):
    vocab = ["reset", "password", "refund", "track", "order"]
    v = np.array([1.0 if w in text.lower() else 0.0 for w in vocab])
    n = np.linalg.norm(v)
    return v / n if n else v

def model_generate(query):
    return f"generated answer for: {query}"

def answer(query, threshold=0.9):
    if query in exact:                       # 1) exact, free, safe
        return exact[query]
    q = embed(query)                         # 2) semantic fallback
    for vec, ans in sem_store:
        if float(np.dot(q, vec)) >= threshold:
            return ans
    resp = model_generate(query)             # 3) miss -> real call
    exact[query] = resp
    sem_store.append((q, resp))
    return resp

if __name__ == "__main__":
    a1 = answer("How do I reset my password?")   # miss -> model
    a2 = answer("How do I reset my password?")   # exact hit
    a3 = answer("How can I reset the password?")  # semantic hit
    print(a2 == a1, a3 == a1)

lineByLine: The exact dict and semantic store hold the two skip-the-model layers.
embed maps a query to a unit vector; here paraphrases share keywords so their vectors are close.
answer checks the exact cache first because it is free and can never return a wrong answer.
On an exact miss it embeds the query and returns a stored answer only if cosine similarity clears the threshold.
If both caches miss, it calls the model and writes the answer into both so future exact and paraphrased repeats hit.
The __main__ block shows an identical repeat hitting the exact cache and a reworded query hitting the semantic cache.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) for the exact lookup; O(k) to scan k stored embeddings on a semantic check (use an ANN index for large k).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(k) for the stored answers and their embeddings.

followUps.question: How would you add TTLs here?
followUps.answer: Store an expires_at with each entry and skip or evict expired ones in both caches, recomputing on the next request.

followUps.question: How does this scale past a linear scan?
followUps.answer: Replace the loop with an approximate-nearest-neighbor index (e.g. a vector database) so semantic lookups stay fast as the store grows.

keyTakeaways: Agents repeat work, so caching is one of the largest cost and latency levers — three layers catch different repetition.
An exact-match cache skips the model on byte-identical requests; it's the cheapest and safest layer to add first.
Provider prompt caching reuses a stable prefix to cut input-token cost on shared-prefix calls, but still makes the call.
A semantic cache embeds the query and reuses answers for near-duplicates above a similarity threshold, capturing paraphrases.
Every cached answer needs a TTL and explicit invalidation on data changes, or the cache silently serves stale, wrong answers.
